text: When a dispute over land (or water, including buildings, markets, fisheries, crops, etc.) is likely to cause a breach of the peace, a District Magistrate or an Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the Government may act. First, the magistrate must be satisfied from a police report or other information that such a dispute exists within his local jurisdiction. He then issues a written order stating the reasons for his satisfaction and directs the parties to appear before his court, either in person or through a pleader, within a time he fixes, and to submit written statements of their respective claims of actual possession. A copy of the order must be served in the manner prescribed for summons and at least one copy must be published at a conspicuous place near the disputed property. After the order is served, the magistrate conducts a hearing without regard to the merits of the parties’ claims: he reads the statements, hears the parties, receives any evidence they produce, may take further evidence if necessary, and then decides which party was in actual possession on the date of the order. (If necessary, the magistrate may also issue a security bond for keeping the peace.)

A statement taken by police is protected only by the rule that the police may not induce or prevent a person from speaking of his own free will.  Section 163 says that no police‑officer or other person shall prevent a person from making a statement of his own free will during an investigation.  By contrast, a confession recorded by a Magistrate must satisfy a number of additional safeguards.  Section 164 requires the Magistrate to explain to the person that he is not bound to confess and that any confession may be used as evidence, to be satisfied that the confession was made voluntarily, and to make a memorandum to that effect.  The confession must be taken in the Magistrate’s presence and hearing, read back to the person and signed by both, and it must be recorded in the manner prescribed in Section 364, which mandates a full, verbatim record of the examination in a language the accused understands.  Thus, police statements are safeguarded only by the prohibition of inducement, whereas magistrate‑recorded confessions are subject to mandatory warnings, verification of voluntariness, formal recording and signing requirements.

text: After a complaint is made, the magistrate must first examine the complainant (Section 200). He then checks whether he has jurisdiction to take cognizance; if he does not, he must return the complaint to the proper court (Section 201(1)) or, if the complaint was not in writing, direct the complainant to the proper court (Section 201(2)). If the magistrate is authorised, he may take cognizance of the offence (Section 202). If, during a complaint case, a police investigation is found to be in progress, the magistrate must stay the proceedings and call for the police report (Section 205D(1)). When the accused is brought before the court, the public prosecutor opens the case by describing the charge and the evidence he will rely on (Section 265B). The court then considers the record and the submissions; if there is no sufficient ground to proceed, it discharges the accused (Section 265C). If the court is of the opinion that there is ground to presume the accused committed an offence, it frames a charge in writing (Section 265D(1)) and reads the charge to the accused, asking whether he pleads guilty (Section 265D(2)). Only after a charge has been framed and the accused’s plea taken does the court proceed to issue process against the accused.

text: A criminal case can be concluded without a full trial in several ways. The court may withdraw the remaining charges after a conviction on one charge, which has the effect of an acquittal on those withdrawn charges (Section 240). A magistrate can discharge an accused if, after reviewing the record and hearing both sides, the charge is found to be groundless (Section 241A). Finally, if after hearing all evidence the court finds there is no evidence that the accused committed the offence, it must record an order of acquittal (Section 265H).

Such withdrawal shall have the effect of an acquittal on such charge or charges, unless the conviction be set aside, in which case the said Court (subject to the order of the Court setting aside the conviction) may proceed with the inquiry into or trial of the charge or charges so withdrawn.

When the accused appears or is brought before the Magistrate, and if the Magistrate, upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith and making such examination, if any, of the accused as the Magistrate thinks necessary and after giving the prosecution and the accused an opportunity of being heard, considers the charge to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.

If, after taking the evidence for the prosecution, examining the accused and hearing the prosecution and the defence on the point, the Court considers that there is no evidence that the accused committed the offence, the Court shall record an order of acquittal.

Those depositions can be admitted as evidence at the inquiry or trial if the witness is dead, incapable of giving evidence, or if obtaining the witness’s attendance would cause unreasonable delay, expense or inconvenience.

text:
After a person is arrested the police may keep him in police custody. A magistrate must first authorise that detention under Section 167. The magistrate must record the reasons for the order (Section 167 (3)) and, if the order is given by a magistrate who is not the Chief Metropolitan or Chief Judicial Magistrate, must forward a copy of the order with the reasons to the superior magistrate (Section 167 (4)); if it is given by a Chief Metropolitan or Chief Judicial Magistrate, the copy is forwarded to the Chief Metropolitan Sessions Judge or Sessions Judge (Section 167 (4A)).

The magistrate may also, under Section 167 (2A), order a medical examination of the accused before he is handed over to police custody and must have the accused produced before the magistrate without unnecessary delay after the period of police custody ends. If any injury or allegation of torture is observed on production, the magistrate must again order a medical examination and act according to law based on the medical report.

Once produced, the magistrate can take cognizance of the offence under Section 190 (1) – either on a complaint, a police report, information from any person, or his own knowledge or suspicion. If, when the accused appears, the magistrate finds that the offence is triable only by the Court of Session, Section 205C requires the magistrate to (a) send the case to the Court of Session, (b) remand the accused to custody until the trial ends, (c) send the case record and evidence to that court, and (d) notify the Public Prosecutor.

The police must forward a report of their investigation to the magistrate under Section 173. A copy of that report must be furnished to the accused before the inquiry or trial begins (Section 173 (4)).

Thus the procedural sequence is: arrest → police custody → magistrate’s authorisation of detention (Section 167) → recording reasons and forwarding order (Section 167 (3)-(4A)) → possible medical examination and production before magistrate (Section 167 (2A)) → magistrate takes cognizance (Section 190) → if exclusive jurisdiction, transfer to Court of Session (Section 205C) → police report provided to magistrate and copy given to accused (Section 173).

text: Magistrates have several duties when a person is arrested and detained. They must receive reports of arrests from police stations (Section 62). They may themselves arrest an offender or order an arrest and can commit the offender to custody, subject to bail provisions (Section 64). A person arrested can be released only on his own bond, on bail, or by a special order of a Magistrate (Section 63). If a Magistrate authorises police custody, he must record the reasons for the order (Section 167(3)) and forward a copy of the order with those reasons to the appropriate senior magistrate (Section 167(4)). The Magistrate may not authorise police detention for more than fifteen days; if longer detention is needed, he must order judicial custody (Section 167). He may also order a medical examination of the accused before handing him over to police custody and must produce the accused before him without delay after police custody ends, ordering further medical examination if injury or torture is alleged (Section 167(2A)).

Section 523 requires any person who may have a claim to appear and establish that claim within the prescribed period. If a claim is proved, the property is returned to that person. If no claim is made, the property becomes the Government’s to dispose of, and the court may order its sale (Section 524(1)). For property that is perishable or likely to decay, the magistrate may direct its sale at any time (Section 525). text: A magistrate must first explain to the person that he is not obliged to confess and that any confession may be used as evidence. The magistrate may only record the confession if, after questioning, he is satisfied it was made voluntarily. The confession is then recorded in writing in the manner prescribed by section 364, signed by both the accused and the magistrate, and the magistrate must certify that it was taken in his presence and hearing and that it is a full and true account. A memorandum stating the explanation given to the accused and the voluntariness of the confession must be placed at the foot of the record.

citations.quote: (3) A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him and no Magistrate shall record any such confession unless, upon questioning the person making it, he has reason to believe that it was made voluntarily; and, when he records any confession, he shall make a memorandum at the foot of such record to the following effect:- "I have explained to (name) that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does so, any confession he may make may be used as evidence against him and I believe that this confession was voluntarily made. It was taken in my presence and hearing, and was read over to the person making it and admitted by him to be correct, and

the truth, the record shall be signed by the accused and the Magistrate or Judge of such Court, and such Magistrate or Judge shall certify under his own hand that the examination was taken in his presence and hearing and that the record contains a full and true account of the statement made by the accused.
